title: He gave his head, not his faith
hook: of his father he writes that he gave his head but not his faith (Bachitar Natak 5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhangani in his words: the cost, the companions, the grace. Your line was through the battle. Whom did you thank by name? Day one thousand two hundred thirty.

At a funeral, the hardest speech belongs to the child. Everyone is waiting to hear what the son or daughter will say: which memory, which word, which part of the life to hold up. Guru Gobind Singh lost his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, to an execution in Delhi. When he came to tell his own life in verse, in Bachitar Natak, he gave his father a few lines. They are short, and every word is chosen.
screen: `THE CHILD'S EULOGY.` → `A SON WHOSE FATHER WAS EXECUTED.` → `A FEW LINES, EVERY WORD CHOSEN.`

segments.voice: Here are the lines, in paraphrase. He protected their forehead mark and their sacred thread, and did a great deed in this dark age. For the sake of the holy, he gave his head, and did not cry out. For the sake of dharma, he did this deed: he gave his head, but not his faith. Look at who the first line protects: their mark, their thread. Those were the signs of another community's worship, not his own. The son remembers his father dying for someone else's right to pray. Then the pair at the center: he gave his head, sis dia, but not his sirar. Sirar is a word Sikhs gloss as his faith, his resolve, the inner thing that can't be handed over. The body could be taken. That couldn't. The poem goes on. The Guru writes that his father would not do tricks to save himself. The people of God, he says in paraphrase, are ashamed to perform a juggler's wonders. No miracle show for an emperor. Just a man who wouldn't move. And then an image: he broke the clay pot of his body on the head of the king of Delhi, and went to the Lord's own place. A clay pot, smashed. Some readers hear in it that the death landed on the one who ordered it, and that the father walked on, unbroken, into God's presence. For a son, this is grief turned into witness. He doesn't dwell on the blade. He tells you what his father kept. Days ago, telling the ninth Guru's stand for freedom of conscience, this path borrowed one of these lines in passing. Today the whole passage gets its own hearing, in his son's voice.
screen: `THEIR MARK, THEIR THREAD.` · `HEAD, BUT NOT SIRAR.` · `NO JUGGLER'S WONDERS.` · `THE CLAY POT BROKEN.` · then, large: `HEAD, NOT FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a principle. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself, gently: what is one thing in me I wouldn't hand over? Not a possession. A principle. Honesty with a child. Fairness at work. Standing up for someone else's right to be who they are. Let it come into focus. Then think of one small place this week where it might be tested, and see yourself holding it. No drama. Just not moving. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
He gave his head. The tenth Guru's words for his father: he gave his head, but not his faith, for the right of others to worship their own way. Today's word.
Your line: head, not faith. Today, keep the principle you named in the sit, in one small moment where letting it go would be easier. Day one thousand two hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Sikhs recall these lines from Bachitar Natak when they remember the martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur, and sis dia par sirar na dia is quoted in katha and kirtan.

fork.setup: you're the son, writing your father's death into your life story. what do you hold up?
options: what he refused to give up, and for whom.
nothing; it's too painful to write.
fork.reveal: Guru Gobind Singh writes that his father protected others' mark and thread, and gave his head but not his faith.

trapdoor: what you thought: a martyr dies for his own people's faith.
what it means: his son writes that he protected the mark and thread of others, and gave his head but not his faith.
what a scholar hears: sis and sirar sit side by side: the head that could be taken, and the resolve that couldn't.
